newsitem.title: CANADA: INTERVIEW - Rogers focused on results.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Rogers focused on results.

text.p: The fuzzy financial picture at Rogers Communications Inc will gradually clear in the coming years, with falling capital expenditures and better operating results, its vice-chairman Phil Lind said on Monday.
But capital spending plans for this year and next remain "very aggressive" -- around the C$920 million level for Rogers Cantel Mobile Communications Inc and the cable division combined.
Spending should fall as soon as Rogers cable finishes deploying its two-way, fiber-coaxial cable hybrid system at the end of 1998.
"It's our hope obviously that we can drive these down as quickly as possible. We recognize that this is one of the biggest complaints about the company," Lind told Reuters in an interview.

"That's concern number one. Concern number two is the operating results -- we're addressing the operating results and we want to limit the capex growth as soon as we possibly can -- get the programs done and reduce the level," he added.

When the two-way, high-speed systems are complete, Rogers' revenues should also start to pick up -- both from additional cable services like pay-per-view and expanded channel offerings and from the ultra-fast Internet service, the Wave.

"So as we develop greater capacity, greater ability for transaction and interactivity and the Wave, I think we have new revenue streams that we will be looking at. But they cost a lot of money," Lind said.
"And that's the debate. But our view is that unless you spend this kind of money, you don't stay competitive. So rather than standing pat, you have to move forward."
Rogers is hunting for someone to head its cable division, which chief executive Ted Rogers has run since last year.

After weathering a stormy 1996, punctuated by the departure of several key executives including cable unit head Colin Watson and chief financial officer Graham Savage, asset sales and widespread criticism about its hefty debt-load, Rogers is back in favor with many analysts.
But some investors remain edgy about the company's future.
Lind said 1997 operating results should improve over last year but positive cash flow remains a distant hope.

Despite Rogers' C$4.6 billion debt load as of December 31, 1996, Lind said its asset sales are largely complete and no equity issues are in the works. To improve the key debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) ratio, Rogers will work on its operating results.
"I think we are comfortable with the shape and definition of the company," Lind said.
Headcount continues to fall at the cable division, with about 100 staff cuts last year and "a few hundred more" are expected this year.
Rogers set aside C$67 million to cover the downsizing in the third quarter of 1996.
Lind said the concerns about Rogers are not entirely prompted by financial concerns.

"It's not just Rogers that's singled out -- there's a lot of debate in the financial community about the future of the cable television industry. Some people think it's going to be very good, and some people continue to be concerned about it," Lind said.
But Rogers' belief in the industry remains unshaken.

"That's the controversy...We're not shying away from it; we're not putting our heads in the sand. It's just that we have a view, and we're going forward on it. It's not a universally shared view," Lind said.

He said Tele-Communications Inc's John Malone may have decided to re-focus his company on expanding capacity rather than on new technologies like the Internet and telephone services. But TCI's smaller, more rural systems are under a more direct threat from satellite television services.
((--Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100))
